title: The next chapter for India’s insurtech is about reach, trust, and retention
content: During calendar year (CY) 2025, Insurtech IPOs and acquisitions hit multi-year highs, even as fresh venture funding into the category grew at a slower rate. Investors are showing more interest in insurance technology but also asking harder questions from companies showing commercial traction. Insurtech, the sector that uses modern technology to make traditional insurance products and processes faster, cheaper, and more personal, is on a rally. India’s insurtech sector is one of the largest in the world, and its choices will shape the next decade of insurance distribution here. According to an October 2025 report by BCG and India InsurTech Association (IIA), India’s insurtech ecosystem has over 150 active players, with cumulative valuations crossing $15.8 billion and revenue reaching $0.9 billion in 2024, a tenfold increase since 2019. The sector has two unicorns, eight players between $100 million and $1 billion and over 45 players with over $1 million. India’s insurtech sector mirrored the global trends, signalling a shift in investor focus to backing businesses with clear paths to profitability and scale, according to the report. Health Insurtech ventures in India accounted for four of the five largest deals and more than 70% of the funding, reflecting their role in driving access, efficiency, and innovation. For much of the past decade, the sector was aiming for scale. This got global capital excited about a market where insurance penetration has been stuck near 3.7% of GDP for years, roughly half the world average. However, the excitement about India’s large addressable market is also a tale of caution, as many insurance distribution companies have had to raise funds regularly to survive. Insurance is difficult to scale responsibly, and the reasons have less to do with technology than with the product itself. For instance, a ride-hailing trip or a food-ordering app proves out its unit economics within days. However, an insurance policy plays out over a year, or five years, or sometimes a lifetime. So, insurtech start-ups cannot simply borrow growth playbooks built for other consumer internet businesses. The sheer cost of distribution in a country where insurance, outside a few urban pockets, is underpenetrated and where regulation is focused more on solvency, claim settlement and disclosure than growth rates, requires an approach that rewards patience over speed. The question, therefore, is what sustainable insurtech looks like amid the challenges the sector faces. To be sure, for years, presence across a large share of India's pincodes was the metric most insurance firms were chasing. It mattered far less whether that customer later bought a different product from the same platform. However, the mindset is slowly changing, with renewal rates and cross-selling turning customer acquisition costs into investments. For instance, an insurance advisor in a small town might spend a Tuesday following up on a claim filed three months earlier, and walking a family through why a certain hospital expense was covered and another was not. That conversation, far more than any app notification or online offers, is what brings the family back when the renewal falls due, and it is often what brings a neighbour or an extended family member to the same advisor looking for a policy of their own. A second shift is toward hybrid distribution, human advisors backed by digital tools, rather than the app-only acquisition approach. The advisor becomes both the acquisition engine and the retention engine, when trust is built through conversation rather than online. That same advisor also chases down missing documents, explaining a rejected claim, or simply answering a call when a policyholder does not know who else to ask. It is this servicing layer, built one interaction at a time, that turns a policy sold into a relationship kept, adding service as its own point, next to Trust and Access, the key pillars of the business. A third, still-emerging shift is that across India's broader insurance sector, from large life insurers to smaller distribution platforms, growth is increasingly being built organically by addressing the expanding population. However, some companies are also expanding inorganically, especially through mergers, acquisitions and foreign investments in order to scale quickly to meet the growing demand. In its early 2026 report on the Indian insurance market, Swiss Re Ltd, a Swiss reinsurance company, predicted the country’s mid-term annual premium growth at 6.9% annually between 2026 and 2030, making India the strongest growing major insurance market globally. Even for the insurtech sector, acquiring an existing agent network or customer base can help in scaling up quickly to tap the market. Perhaps this is the reason why the central government had once considered merging the loss-making state-owned insurers. The centre has since then asked these companies to focus on profitability, with the government monitoring their performance for a possible decision in the future. To be sure, even policy has started nudging the sector towards consolidation. The opening of 100% foreign direct investment into insurance, the recent rationalisation of GST on individual life and health premiums, and the regulator's own emphasis on capital efficiency and faster claim settlements point towards a sector that wants to be judged on outcomes for policyholders and not headlines about funding raised. However, none of this means growth stops mattering, as India remains badly under-insured, and closing that gap needs both existing and new players to push harder. Domestic rating agency, ICRA Ltd., in its April 2026 report on the Indian insurance sector, said it expects the individual New Business Premium (NBP) to rise by 9.4-9.9% to Rs 2.02-2.03 trillion in FY 2027, driven by private insurers. NBP is the total money collected from newly sold insurance policies industry wide. The rating agency expects overall NBP to rise by 7.8-8.2% to Rs 4.95-4.97 trillion in FY2027 from Rs 4.60 trillion in FY 2026 and Rs 3.97 trillion in FY 2025. Having spent close to a decade building an insurance distribution business from a handful of towns into a nationwide network, we believe the insurtech companies that matter five years from now will be the ones that create real value for this growing ecosystem, while also treating every funding round as a fuel for growing the business. (Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

title: VC funding dips in September despite big deals; More voices join the lineup at TechSparks 2026
content: Dear Reader, PhysicsWallah will no longer lend to students directly. The edtech company’s wholly-owned subsidiary FinZ Finance has agreed to sell a Rs 95.79 crore loan portfolio to Auxilo Finserve, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on education finance. This is part of PhysicsWallah’s strategic move to focus on its core business and reduce balance-sheet and credit risks associated with lending. Going forward, lending will be facilitated through regulated third-party NBFCs. In other news, TVS Automobile Solutions has raised Rs 425 crore in a Series D round of funding led by CE-Invests, the investment arm of UAE-based Crescent Enterprises. The funding will be used to expand the company’s myTVS aftermarket brand in overseas markets, starting with MENA. Meanwhile, ecommerce marketplace Flipkart has picked up a minority stake in global B2B travel tech startup TravClan to strengthen international holiday offerings across Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel and expand access to global suppliers and destination support. This caught some investors off guard, especially as grey market trading had earlier indicated a 3% listing gain. The benefits outweigh the risks, he argued. “We believe that ​the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman said in an interview with Politico's tech-centric newsletter Decoded . title: Beyond Appliances raises Rs 110 Cr in Series B round led by Fireside Ventures
content: Kitchen appliances brand Beyond Appliances has raised Rs 110 crore in a Series B round of funding led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from Dharana Capital and other investors. The Bengaluru-based company will use the funding towards research and development and its new manufacturing plant. The startup will also use the capital to enter new product categories in the kitchen appliances space and strengthen its presence across its existing portfolio. Beyond Appliances' co-founder & CEO Eshwar K Vikas said, “We believe the next big shift in the appliance industry will come from building products that are not only technologically advanced but are fundamentally designed around how Indian households cook and live. The opportunity ahead is significantly larger, and this investment gives us the ability to pursue it with greater ambition.” Founded in 2024 by Eshwar K Vikas and Rakesh Patil, Beyond Appliances follows an omnichannel strategy with a retail presence in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad and a manufacturing facility is in Bengaluru. Its range of products include Android chimneys, Plug-N-Play chimneys, smart hobs, and cooktops. Beyond Appliances plans to expand its offline presence to 10 more cities over the next three years. The company says 15% of its revenue comes through customer referrals. Rakesh Patil, Co-Founder & CTO, Beyond Appliances, said, “Over the last two years, our R&D teams have worked closely with consumers to identify everyday challenges in Indian kitchens and translate those insights into products that are genuinely different.” Shuchi Pandya, Principal, Fireside Ventures, said, “ Very few early-stage brands demonstrate the depth of fundamentals that Beyond Appliances has built at this stage of its journey. From technology-led products and a growing omnichannel presence to strong in-house R&D and manufacturing capabilities, the company has taken a thoughtful approach to building a differentiated consumer brand.”

title: Why finance teams need to think in systems
content: Finance has always had a role beyond recording transactions. It is involved in planning, controls, treasury, risk, and decision-making. What is changing is the extent to which finance teams are also involved in the systems through which financial activity takes place. A customer's payment information can now move through a website or app, a payment system, an invoicing platform, a bank account, and an accounting system before it appears in a financial report. If those systems do not communicate, someone has to fill the gaps: checking transactions, moving data, downloading reports, and matching records manually. As businesses grow, it becomes harder to manage. Finance teams are becoming more involved in how these processes are designed. They are looking at where data comes from, where it needs to go, which steps can be automated, and how different systems should work together. Finance remains responsible for financial control, visibility, and decision-making. But fulfilling that responsibility increasingly requires an understanding of the systems behind the numbers. From recording transactions to designing workflows Consider a typical payment. A customer pays an invoice online. The payment needs to be recorded, the invoice updated, the money sent to the right bank account, and the transaction eventually reconciled with the accounting records. When each step sits in a different system, finance teams can end up doing much of this work manually. The same applies as businesses add subscriptions, recurring payments, payment links, marketplaces, or physical locations. Finance may also have to manage refunds, disputes, settlements, payouts, and multiple banking relationships. So payments are becoming part of a wider financial workflow, not a series of individual transactions. Technology can take some of the repetitive work out of this process. More importantly, it lets finance teams look at the workflow as a whole. Can a successful payment automatically update an invoice? Can payment information move into accounting without being entered again? Can a failed transaction trigger the next step without someone having to monitor it? These are questions about how financial processes should work, and technology can help make them happen. Finance starts thinking in systems Accounting and financial controls remain at the centre of the function, but finance professionals also need to be comfortable with data, digital systems, and the way information moves between them. A 2025 Wolters Kluwer survey of 100 senior finance executives in India found that 74% ranked digital transformation as a top priority, while 66% prioritized workflow automation. The survey also identified fragmented systems and data silos as challenges for finance teams. Finance professionals do not need to become software developers. But they do need to understand what a system can do, where a process is breaking down, and what should happen when two systems need to exchange information. As routine work becomes more automated, finance teams can spend more time on analysis, planning, problem-solving, and working with other parts of the business. That also brings them closer to decisions about how processes are built, how different systems connect, and where technology can improve them. Also Read When payments grow beyond the gateway Connecting financial systems An API allows different software applications to exchange information and interact with each other. For finance teams, this means that payment information related to payments does not have to stop at the payment platform. Transaction information can move into systems handling invoices, accounting, orders, or customer records. For example, once a customer completes a payment, that transaction information can pass to another application, which can update the relevant financial record or trigger the next step in the workflow. Zoho Payments provides REST-based APIs that allow businesses to incorporate payment functionality into their applications. It also supports webhooks, which can send real-time notifications when events such as successful or failed payments, refunds, and payouts take place. For finance, the value is in what these connections let the business do. Payment collection, invoicing, and reconciliation can become one workflow, instead of separate activities that require moving information between systems. Building finance operations that can scale A process that works when a business handles a few dozen transactions can become a bottleneck as the number of customers, invoices, payment methods, and bank transactions grows. More manual work also creates more opportunities for errors and mismatches. Connected systems can help businesses handle more volume without increasing manual work at the same rate. They can reduce the need to move information between systems manually, limit mismatches, and give finance teams better visibility into financial activity. Zoho Payments is one example of this connected approach.When used with Zoho Books, payment information can flow into the accounting workflow, helping businesses record collections, track settlements, and reconcile transactions. For businesses with more specific requirements, APIs provide another way to connect payment functionality with existing applications and workflows. The aim is to make payments, invoices, and reconciliation work together rather than treating them as separate tasks. This can give finance teams more control over how financial information moves through the business, while reducing the amount of manual intervention as transaction volumes grow. The finance team will still close the books, manage cash, and oversee reporting. But it is also likely to have a greater role in deciding which systems connect, which tasks should be automated, and how financial data moves from one part of the business to another. Finance isn’t becoming IT. But understanding the numbers increasingly means understanding the systems that move them.

title: 7 Books that teach you how to think under pressure
content: Pressure is an unavoidable part of life. Whether it arrives as a looming deadline, a difficult decision, a personal setback, or an unexpected crisis, the ability to think clearly under stress often determines how well we respond. While pressure can cloud judgment and trigger emotional reactions, it can also become an opportunity to develop resilience, focus, and confidence. The good news is that clear thinking under pressure is not simply an inborn trait. It is a skill that can be learned and strengthened over time. Some of the best insights on decision-making, mental toughness, emotional control, and resilience can be found in books that explore how people navigate challenging situations. Here are seven books that can help you stay calm, think clearly, and make better decisions when the stakes are high. 1. The Comfort Crisis by Michael Easter Modern life often shields us from discomfort, but growth happens when we learn to face challenges. Easter explores how embracing controlled hardship can build resilience, confidence, and the ability to stay calm under pressure. 2. The Art of Clear Thinking by Hasard Lee Written by a former U.S. Air Force fighter pilot, this book examines how people can make better decisions in high-stakes situations. Lee shares practical strategies for reducing panic, evaluating risks, and thinking clearly when every second counts. 3. Building a Second Brain by Tiago Forte Pressure often comes from information overload. Forte's book teaches readers how to organise knowledge effectively so they can think more clearly, make decisions faster, and r educe mental stress during demanding situations. Also Read 7 daily habits that quietly build lasting confidence 4. The Scout Mindset by Julia Galef Galef argues that the best thinkers approach problems with curiosity rather than defensiveness. The book teaches readers how to evaluate situations objectively, challenge assumptions, and make better decisions under pressure. 5. The Courage to Be Disliked by Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga Based on the ideas of psychologist Alfred Adler, this book explores how people can stop seeking constant approval from others. It offers insights into handling criticism, pressure, and anxiety with greater confidence. 6. Peak Mind by Amishi P. Jha Neuroscientist Amishi Jha explains how attention works and why stress can impair decision-making. The book provides research-backed techniques for improving focus and maintaining clarity during challenging moments. 7. The Extended Mind by Annie Murphy Paul This book challenges the idea that thinking happens only inside our heads. Paul explores how our surroundings, relationships, and physical actions can help us solve problems and make better decisions when under pressure. Final thoughts Pressure has a way of revealing our habits, thought patterns, and emotional responses. While stressful situations cannot always be avoided, our ability to navigate them can improve through practice and learning. These seven books approach the subject from different angles- psychology, philosophy, leadership, history, and personal development- but they share a common lesson: clear thinking under pressure comes from preparation, perspective, and resilience. The more we develop those qualities, the better equipped we become to handle life's most demanding moments.

title: Quantum computing and AI firm QpiAI secures Rs 50 Cr debt financing from InnoVen Capital
content: Quantum computing and artificial intelligence company QpiAI has secured Rs 50 crore in debt financing from InnoVen Capital India Fund II, with the Bengaluru startup allotting 5,000 Series B non-convertible debentures to the fund, according to RoC filings. The debentures have a face value of Rs 1 lakh each, carry a 13.85% annual coupon, and are secured. The transaction was approved by QpiAI’s board on August 28. Entrackr was the first to report the debt financing. The transaction adds debt alongside QpiAI’s earlier equity fundraising. The company had raised $6.5 million in a pre-Series A round in June 2024, led by YourNest and SIDBI Venture Capital, followed by a $32 million Series A in July 2025 led by Avataar Ventures and the National Quantum Mission. That puts its disclosed equity funding at $38.5 million before the latest debt round. Companies typically use venture debt to add capital without issuing new shares, thereby limiting ownership dilution for founders and existing investors. It can also provide additional runway between equity rounds and help finance growth while a company works towards commercial milestones. Also Read QpiAI opens ‘Asia’s largest’ quantum chip foundry, targets 10,000-qubit processors The financing comes as QpiAI pushes further into quantum hardware and software. However, the company has not disclosed a specific use for the Rs 50 crore proceeds in the board resolution; so the funds cannot be tied to a particular project. Founded in 2019, QpiAI develops vertically integrated quantum systems and AI platforms for areas including drug discovery, materials science, manufacturing, logistics and finance. It launched its 25-qubit QpiAI-Indus system in 2025 and subsequently unveiled a 64-qubit processor. The company has previously stated its goal to move quantum technology beyond experimentation and towards commercial use. Founder and CEO Nagendra Nagaraja has said that “markets are ripe for utility-scale quantum computers with logical qubits,” referring to more advanced machines built around error-corrected qubits. The latest financing arrives as India builds policy and infrastructure around emerging technologies. The National Quantum Mission, approved in April 2023 with an outlay of Rs 6,003.65 crore over eight years, is aimed at developing quantum computing, communication, sensing, materials and devices, including intermediate-scale machines with 50 to 1,000 physical qubits. title: 7 Books that teach you why rich people think differently
content: Most people assume that becoming rich is simply a matter of earning more money. Yet many people with high incomes struggle financially, while others quietly build substantial wealth over time. The difference often lies in how they think. Wealthy people tend to view money, opportunities, risk, and time differently. They focus on building assets, making long-term decisions, and developing habits that compound over years rather than seeking quick rewards. While no book can guarantee financial success, some offer valuable insights into the mindset and principles that have shaped generations of entrepreneurs, investors, and self-made millionaires. Here are seven books that explain why rich people think differently and what the rest of us can learn from them. 1. Rich Dad Poor Dad by Robert Kiyosaki Few books have influenced conversations about money as much as Rich Dad Poor Dad . Through the contrasting lessons of two father figures, Kiyosaki introduces readers to a different way of thinking about wealth. The book challenges the traditional belief that a good job alone leads to financial freedom. Instead, it emphasises financial education, building assets, and making money work for you rather than constantly working for money. One of its biggest lessons is that wealthy people focus on acquiring assets that generate income, while many others spend most of their earnings on liabilities. 2. The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel Many people know what they should do with money but still make poor financial decisions. Morgan Housel explores why. Rather than focusing on complex investment strategies, the book examines the role of behaviour, emotions, patience, and decision-making in wealth creation. It argues that financial success is often less about intelligence and more about habits and discipline . The book shows that wealthy individuals understand the power of long-term thinking and compounding, while others often allow fear, ego, or impatience to dictate their choices. 3. Think and Grow Rich by Napoleon Hill First published in 1937, this classic remains one of the most influential books on success and wealth. Hill studied the lives and habits of highly successful individuals and identified common principles such as persistence, goal-setting, belief, and focused action. The book argues that wealth creation begins with a clear purpose and a strong desire to achieve it. While some ideas reflect the era in which it was written, its central message remains relevant: successful people often think differently long before they achieve different results. 4. The Intelligent Investor by Benjamin Graham Widely regarded as one of the greatest investing books ever written, The Intelligent Investor teaches readers how to think rationally about money. Graham encourages investors to focus on value, remain patient, and avoid emotional decisions driven by market excitement or panic. The wealthy often understand that preserving capital and making thoughtful decisions are just as important as making money. This book explains why emotional discipline is a crucial part of long-term financial success . Also Read 5 Lessons from The Psychology of Money about wealth 5. The Richest Man in Babylon by George S. Clason Written as a collection of parables set in ancient Babylon, this classic presents timeless principles of wealth creation. Its lessons are remarkably simple: save a portion of every income, control spending, invest wisely, and allow money to grow over time. The book demonstrates that many financial truths remain unchanged regardless of the era. Wealth often begins with small, consistent actions repeated for years. 6. How Rich People Think by Steve Siebold After studying wealthy individuals for decades, Steve Siebold set out to understand what separates their thinking from that of the average person. The book contrasts common beliefs about money with the attitudes often found among self-made millionaires. It explores topics such as responsibility, opportunity, risk-taking, and personal growth. Its central argument is that financial success is heavily influenced by mindset and that changing the way you think can change the way you approach opportunities and wealth. Final thoughts Rich people are not necessarily smarter than everyone else, but they often approach money with a different perspective. They focus on ownership rather than consumption, long-term growth rather than instant gratification, and opportunities rather than limitations. These seven books offer different viewpoints on wealth creation, but they share a common message: financial success begins with how you think. Changing your mindset may not make you rich overnight, but it can help you make better decisions that compound over time.

title: VC funding in September dips 8.3% year on year
content: Venture capital funding into Indian startups saw an 8.3% year-on-year dip in September, despite four $100 million deals. However, VC funding rose 15.5% compared to August, revealing the divergent trends in capital inflow into the startup ecosystem. The total VC funding for September this year was $1.139 billion, compared to $1.242 billion in the same month last year, according to YourStory Research. The VC funding in August 2026 was $986 million. There were some positives in September. The month marked the third time that VC funding crossed $1 billion this year. The other two times were in February ($1.40 billion) and July ($2 billion). Four deals crossed the $100 million mark in September: Pixxel ($100 million), DMI ($152 million), Simple Energy ($182 million), and SiMa ai ($150 million). The other notable deal was Ultrahuman ($70 million). These five deals accounted for $654 million. This shows that it is the large deals that provide a boost to the funding momentum. Between July and September of 2026, the total VC funding raised was $2.92 billion, 2% higher than the $2.86 billion raised in the similar period last year. Surprisingly, the early-stage category showed the highest traction at $557 million, followed by growth stage at $331 million. Generally, it is the late-stage startups that raise the largest quantum of funding, but in September, the category raised just $85 million. The fintech segment raised the highest amount of funding in September at $251 million followed by electric vehicles at $222 million. Among the cities, Bengaluru was at the number one spot at $666 million followed by Delhi-NCR at $211 million and Mumbai at $149 million. This has been a key challenge in the Indian startup ecosystem with entrepreneurial activity not really percolating to the other metros of the country. It has been a mixed bag for the Indian startup ecosystem in the nine months of the year with total funding at $9.8 billion. It remains to be seen whether the remaining three months of the year will help total funding cross 2025's number. Last year, the total funding raised was $12.1 billion. Current trends indicate that 2026 may show a marginal improvement over 2025 in terms of overall funding. However, it will be challenging given that the last three months of the year are generally a period of slower activity. However, one positive trend is the fundraise by a few Indian AI startups in recent times, and this bodes well for the overall startup ecosystem.

title: Bhavish Aggarwal pledges 4.32% stake to back Ola Electric’s Rs 1,000 Cr rights issue
content: Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal has stepped up to back the company’s upcoming Rs 1,000 crore rights issue, pledging a 4.32% stake in the EV maker to fund his participation. The move comes days after Ola Electric’s board greenlit the plan to raise fresh capital through partly paid-up shares and appointed Deepa Bansal as its new compliance chief to bolster governance. According to stock exchange filings on Sunday, Aggarwal pledged 20 crore shares against non-convertible debentures issued by Krutrim Data Centre Private Limited—a non-operative promoter entity owned by Aggarwal—to CTL Trusteeship Limited. The company clarified that no shares are being sold, no other pledges exist on his holdings, and Aggarwal will subscribe to the issue on the same terms as all other shareholders. Unlike many tech founders whose ownership dilutes quickly after going public, Aggarwal and his promoter group still hold about a third of Ola Electric. By subscribing to his share of the rights issue, Aggarwal ensures his ownership stake stays intact once the new shares hit the market. The fresh cash push arrives at a high-stakes moment for the Bengaluru-based EV manufacturer. Sharper competition from legacy brands like TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto, and Hero MotoCorp, along with rival Ather Energy, recently dragged Ola Electric down to fifth place in monthly vehicle registrations. In Q1 FY27, revenue fell to Rs 455 crore from Rs 828 crore a year earlier, though losses narrowed to Rs 336 crore. Having raised Rs 780 crore through a qualified institutional placement in June, the Rs 1,000 crore rights issue gives Ola Electric another balance-sheet cushion as it works to defend its market position. (Disclaimer: Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory, is an independent director at Ola Electric.)

title: PhysicsWallah retreats from direct student lending as FinZ loan book heads to Auxilo
content: Edtech firm PhysicsWallah (PW) has moved decisively to reduce its exposure to direct student lending, with its wholly-owned subsidiary FinZ Finance agreeing to sell a Rs 95.79 crore loan portfolio to Auxilo Finserve, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on education finance. The deal covers a substantial or major part of FinZ’s loan book and is expected to result in a partial closure of its lending operations, PW said, adding the transition of the loans and borrowers should be completed within 60 days. The significance of this move lies in the speed of the reversal. In its October 4 filing, PW said “the closure of substantial/major part of the total loan portfolio of FinZ Finance forms part of a broader strategic realignment,” aimed at focusing on the core business , optimising capital allocation and reducing balance-sheet and credit risks. Going forward, lending will be facilitated through regulated third-party NBFCs instead of being carried directly through FinZ, the Noida-based firm noted. On May 27, PW’s Audit Committee approved an investment of approximately Rs 120 crore in FinZ through a rights issue to fund working capital and expand the business. FinZ had received its RBI licence in September 2025 and had only recently begun operations. In the May 27 earnings call, management said the model was built on an earlier partnership with an external NBFC that had disbursed nearly Rs 200 crore over about two years, with less than 1% NPA, or non-performing assets, and around 70% of loans going to PW students. Asked whether new loans would sit on PW’s balance sheet, management replied, “Yes, so we got NBFC license from RBI and yes, we will be giving loans through that NBFC only.” The market reaction then provided a signal as after the Rs 120 crore investment announcement, PW shares fell nearly 18% over five sessions. On June 4, after PW announced that it would instead work with regulated third-party NBFCs, the stock surged as much as 17.75% on the BSE. That does not establish that investors alone triggered the change, and PW has not said that they did. But the sequence strongly suggests that capital allocation and financial-risk concerns had become important considerations. Earlier, PW had also shifted its K-12 strategy towards an asset-light model after investor questions around capital-intensive expansion. Recently, The CapTable wrote about how the edtech firm is finding that revenue and profit are not enough. Investors are rewarding restraint, and they want to know exactly where the next leg of growth will come from. The listed company’s explanation for the lending reversal was explicit. Co-founder Prateek Maheshwari had said , “Our lending business is best left to regulated third-party NBFCs who have created robust underwriting capabilities.” He also added that the company had received feedback from partners and that it had a fiduciary responsibility to revisit the earlier decision in the interests of capital allocation and shareholders. The June-quarter financial notes subsequently recorded that Rs 120 crore had been invested in FinZ, so the reversal did not simply cancel the capital injection. The wider lending environment also favours regulated intermediaries. RBI’s Digital Lending Directions, 2025 strengthened requirements for platforms working with multiple lenders, including clearer presentation of loan offers, interest costs and tenures, while its framework keeps regulated entities responsible for their lending arrangements. Education finance itself remains a growing market, with Crisil expecting NBFC education-loan assets to rise 20% in FY27, although that forecast largely concerns higher education and is not directly comparable with PW’s short-duration course financing. Byju’s provides the cautionary backdrop. Its India CFO had said in January 2024 that 25-30% of the company’s business had come through customer loans, but NBFCs had stopped lending to its customers after audit delays, disrupting the earlier model and affecting collections. Byju’s subsequent collapse involved much broader financial, governance and lender disputes. Its insolvency battle followed a major dispute with lenders and a series of other setbacks. The FinZ loan sale looks less like a retreat from student financing itself than a decision to separate education distribution from credit risk as PW can continue connecting students with lenders, while regulated financial institutions carry the lending exposure.

title: From fintech to semiconductors, TechSparks 2026 brings more voices to the New Tech Order
content: Technology is changing how businesses are built, products reach consumers, and new industries take shape. At TechSparks 2026 , YourStory’s flagship startup and technology summit, founders, investors, technology leaders, and policymakers will come together under the theme ‘The New Tech Order’. The three-day summit will take place in Bengaluru from October 13-15. Karnataka ministers Priyank Kharge , Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, and Krishna Byre Gowda , Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, will join the conversations, alongside Pratyaya Amrit , Chief Secretary, Government of Bihar. Also Read TechSparks 2026 returns, centring on ‘The New Tech Order’ The lineup also includes entrepreneurs and technology leaders working across consumer businesses, healthcare, fintech, deeptech, semiconductors and defence. Here are some of the speakers joining TechSparks 2026: Ananth Narayanan Ananth Narayanan, Founder and CEO of BRND.ME, has built and scaled consumer businesses across categories. He was previously CEO of Myntra and Co-founder of Medlife. He will bring his experience in building consumer businesses and working at the intersection of technology and brands to the TechSparks stage. Mohit Bhatnagar Mohit Bhatnagar is Managing Director at Peak XV. His work in venture capital spans investments across consumer, technology, and other sectors, giving him a view of founders building companies as well as investors backing them. Kalavathi G V Kalavathi G V is Executive Director and Head of the Global Development Center at Siemens Healthineers. The Bengaluru centre works on technology and R&D for the company’s global healthcare business. Rahul Chari Rahul Chari is Founder and CPTO at PhonePe. As co-founder, he has been closely involved in building the company’s technology and product functions as it has expanded its digital payments and financial services business. Bharat Mandot Bharat Mandot is Founder and Chairman of Stelcore Group. The group works across commerce and supply-chain businesses, with its operations spanning Stelcore Commerce and Stelcore Supply Chain. Shweta Rajpal Kohli Shweta Rajpal Kohli is President and CEO of Startup Policy Forum (SPF), which works with India's startup ecosystem on policy and advocacy. Her work sits at the intersection of startups, businesses, and government. Hareesh Chandrasekar Hareesh Chandrasekar is CEO and Co-founder of Agnit Semiconductors. The company is working on semiconductor technologies, including gallium nitride, with applications across areas such as telecom and power electronics. Ankit Maheshwari Ankit Maheshwari is Founder and CTO of Innovaccer, a healthcare technology company. His work focuses on using technology and AI to address challenges around healthcare data and delivery. Natasha Tuli Natasha Tuli is Founder of Soulflower, a personal-care brand built around natural ingredients and essential oils. She has led the brand as it has expanded its range of products across hair, skin and wellness. Arvind Lakshmikumar Arvind Lakshmikumar is Co-founder, MD, and CEO of Tonbo Imaging, which develops imaging and sensing technologies for defence and other applications. The TechSparks 2026 lineup also features Nupur Goenka, Executive Director, Tally Solutions; Ankit Bagaria, Co-founder and CEO, Loopworm; Vikas Brahmavar, Founder and Director, Boson Whitewater; Chetan Maini, Chairman and Co-founder, SUN Mobility; Angad Daryani, Founder and CEO, Praan; Nikhil Rajpal, Founder, Qubo; Akshay Shekhar, CEO and Co-founder, Kazam; and Sharat Chandra, Founder, EmpowerEdge Ventures. title: Andhra Pradesh, PanIIT partner for Rs 500-Cr deeptech fund; An intralogistics business that serves 25 countries
content: Dear Reader, Industry experts argue India must develop its own AI safety framework tailored to its unique languages, scale, and application-focused ecosystem, rather than copy the newly signed White House Accord on Super Intelligence. While top US tech firms such as OpenAI, Meta, Google, and xAI recently committed to voluntary internal controls, external audits, and oversight teams under the US pact, Indian leaders like Nasscom Chairman Srikanth Velamakanni emphasize that India needs a customised, multi-stakeholder approach. Meanwhile, India’s top IT services firms are expected to post muted revenue growth (0.5–1% quarter-on-quarter) and stable margins for Q2 FY27 due to tight discretionary client budgets and prolonged decision cycles amid geopolitical tensions. While UnearthInsight expects Q2 performance to mirror a sluggish Q1, Gartner sees a slight uptick driven by older contract wins transitioning into revenue. Overall, analysts say that market cautiousness persists, with key focus turning to conversion rates from deal pipelines to revenue and the deflationary impact of AI on traditional IT services. Moving on to the world of electric vehicles, researchers are now looking at why some people feel motion sickness in an EV while others don’t. One of the possible reasons could be that humans have got accustomed to the sound of engines with movement. The silence in electric cars could trigger motion sickness , BBC reports. Other reasons include the braking mechanism in these cars as well as the way they accelerate and decelerate. In Focus ICYMI: An intralogistics business that serves 25 countries Over the past decade, Addverb has scaled from a five-member team into a global intralogistics player with over 1,000 employees, 300+ clients, and operations across 25 countries. Addverb is currently expanding its R&D into "physical AI" and aims to double its revenue while expanding its global presence to 100 countries over the next decade. title: AceVector makes weak market debut, shares list 11.5% below issue price
content: Shares of AceVector Ltd., the parent company of Snapdeal, stumbled on their stock market debut on Monday, October 5, opening at a notable discount on both the NSE and BSE. The stock listed at Rs 28.32 on the NSE and Rs 28.30 on the BSE, down roughly 11.5% from its issue price of Rs 32. The weak debut caught some investors off guard, especially as grey market trading had previously indicated a modest 3% listing gain. The company raised Rs 420 crore at the upper end of its Rs 30 to Rs 32 price band, giving it a market capitalisation of Rs 1,540.05 crore. The issue included a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 287 crore alongside an offer for sale component of Rs 133 crore, allowing early investors like SoftBank subsidiary Starfish and Nexus Venture Partners to offload part of their holdings. By the time bidding closed on September 29, the offering was subscribed 5.07 times overall, driven largely by high-net-worth individuals, while retail and institutional quotas saw steady participation. Ahead of the main opening, AceVector had already secured Rs 189 crore from a group of anchor investors at Rs 32 per share. Funds like Negen Undiscovered Value Fund, Singularity Growth Opportunities, and Turnaround Opportunities Fund took up significant portions of the anchor book, alongside a mix of other domestic and offshore funds. SoftBank's Starfish remains the company's largest shareholder with a 30.11% stake, followed by co-founders Kunal Bahl and Rohit Kumar Bansal. The Gurugram-based firm operates a digital ecosystem that spans Snapdeal, SaaS provider Unicommerce eSolutions, and direct-to-consumer brands under Stellaro Brands. While the business remains in the red, it managed to narrow its net loss to Rs 60.7 crore in FY26 from Rs 139.2 crore the previous year, with operating revenue rising 29.2% to Rs 510.4 crore. AceVector plans to use the bulk of its Rs 287 crore fresh capital to ramp up marketing efforts, upgrade its technology stack, and explore strategic acquisitions.

title: TVS Automobile Solutions raises Rs 425 Cr from UAE investor to expand myTVS brand
content: TVS Automobile Solutions, which owns the omnichannel automotive aftermarket brand myTVS, has raised Rs 425 crore in a Series D round of funding led by CE-Invests, the investment arm of UAE-based Crescent Enterprises. TVS Automobile Solutions is part of the $3 billion TVS Mobility Group. Prior to this funding round, myTVS had raised around Rs 690 crore, comprising Rs 203 crore from Lingotto (Exor) in 2022 and Rs 487 Cr from Castrol in 2023. According to a statement, the latest funding will support myTVS' overseas expansion with initial focus on the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) markets, where both the companies see potential to adapt and scale its technology and capabilities for mobility and fleet businesses. For CE-Invests, this partnership provides an opportunity to leverage myTVS' technology platform and capabilities in the automotive aftermarket in the Middle East. For myTVS, CE-Invests brings deep regional market understanding and business networks that can support the identification and development of new opportunities across MENA. The statement noted that myTVS has developed an integrated automotive aftermarket platform that combines digital capabilities with a physical service network for OEMs and EV manufacturers to access a broad range of vehicle service and maintenance solutions. R Dinesh, Director, TVS Automobile Solutions said, “ This investment is a further proof that this technology-led platform is capable of delivering a similar experience in other markets. This will further enable the company to scale up its operations in India and the MENA region and continue to maintain its profitable growth.” According to the statement, myTVS has achieved EBITDA breakeven in FY26 and expects its business to grow 25–35% in the near term. The company is accelerating investments in AI and technology to support this growth, strengthen the scalability of its platform, and build the capabilities required for its next phase of expansion. Badr Jafar, CEO of Crescent Enterprises said, “ When India’s scale, talent and innovation connect with the UAE’s capital, infrastructure and regional reach, each market becomes a platform for the other’s growth. That reciprocal model creates value far beyond either country and reflects principles that have long shaped Crescent Enterprises’ investment and partnership strategy.” Edited by Swetha Kannan

title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 5, 2026)
content: From PanIIT Alumni India and the Andhra Pradesh government’s plan to create a Rs 500 crore venture fund focused on deeptech companies, to Ola Electric’s Chairman, Bhavish Aggarwal pledging a 4.32% stake in the company to raise funds, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors. Featured Stories PhysicsWallah retreats from direct student lending Edtech firm PhysicsWallah (PW) has moved decisively to reduce its exposure to direct student lending, with its wholly-owned subsidiary FinZ Finance agreeing to sell a Rs 95.79 crore loan portfolio to Auxilo Finserve, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on education finance. The deal covers a substantial or major part of FinZ’s loan book and is expected to result in a partial closure of its lending operations, PW said, adding the transition of the loans and borrowers should be completed within 60 days. The significance of this move lies in the speed of the reversal. Read more Latest news Bhavish Aggarwal pledges 4.32% stake to back Ola Electric Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal has stepped up to back the company’s upcoming Rs 1,000 crore rights issue, pledging a 4.32% stake in the EV maker to fund his participation. The move comes days after Ola Electric’s board greenlit the plan to raise fresh capital through partly paid-up shares and appointed Deepa Bansal as its new compliance chief to bolster governance. According to stock exchange filings on Sunday, Aggarwal pledged 20 crore shares against non-convertible debentures issued by Krutrim Data Centre Private Limited—a non-operative promoter entity owned by Aggarwal—to CTL Trusteeship Limited. The company clarified that no shares are being sold, no other pledges exist on his holdings, and Aggarwal will subscribe to the issue on the same terms as all other shareholders. Read more Other news DigiCert launches global Partner Network to accelerate digital trust and quantum readiness DigiCert has introduced the DigiCert Partner Network, a global initiative designed to help partners deliver, manage, and scale digital trust solutions across six distinct business models, including a dedicated MSP Program. Built on the DigiCert ONE platform, the network enables partners to move beyond basic certificate lifecycle automation into high-growth areas like PKI modernisation, software and device security, AI trust, and post-quantum cryptography transition, unlocking recurring, services-led revenue streams. Table Space expands Hyderabad portfolio, partners DoorDash Table Space, India’s largest flexible workspace operator by leased area, has expanded its Hyderabad footprint to 1.56 million sq. ft. across eight years. As the market expands beyond established hubs like HITEC City into emerging corridors like Neopolis, global local-commerce platform DoorDash has chosen Table Space to establish its first India talent hub. Table Space will oversee the leasing, design, build, and management of DoorDash’s initial and long-term HITEC City offices. This collaboration highlights Table Space’s enterprise-focused managed-office model. Nationally, GCCs account for 53.50% of the company’s leased area, positioning Table Space to capture growing global demand across key Indian commercial hubs. WeWork India expands Bengaluru and Pune footprint with 4,500+ desks WeWork India Management Limited has expanded its footprint by opening two new centres in key commercial hubs: WeWork Infinix Palladium in Bengaluru and WeWork Millennium Towers in Pune. Together, the locations add approximately 2.25 lakh sq. ft. and over 4,500 desks to the company’s national portfolio, responding to rising demand in self-sustained urban corridors. Spanning 1.7 lakh sq. ft. near the Singayyanapalya Metro Station, the standalone Whitefield centre in Bengaluru offers 3,100+ desks tailored for large enterprise scale. In Pune, the LEED Platinum-certified Wakad facility adds 55,000 sq. ft. and 1,400 desks, capitalizing on proximity to the Hinjewadi tech hub and the Mumbai-Pune Expressway."" Razorpay teams up with OpenAI to launch ChatGPT ads for Indian brands Fintech giant Razorpay has partnered with OpenAI to help Indian businesses run ad campaigns on ChatGPT via its Razorpay Engage platform. The collaboration enables brands to optimize product catalogues, manage feeds, and run targeted, AI-driven campaigns as consumers shift toward conversational product discovery over traditional keyword searches. Prominent early adopters include Tanishq, Tata Neu, Fastrack, Axis Max Life, Traya, Shaadi.com, Palmonas, and NMIMS. Powered by an AI agent with human oversight, Razorpay Engage handles campaign setup, catalogue readiness, and performance tracking, allowing local businesses to seamlessly tap into conversational AI discovery without building in-house technical infrastructure. Snabbit appoints rormer PhonePe executive Ramesh Srinivasan as Head of Growth and Revenue Quick home services platform Snabbit has named former PhonePe marketing leader Ramesh Srinivasan as Head of Growth and Revenue. Srinivasan, who previously held senior roles at Flipkart and PhonePe, will oversee customer acquisition, retention, brand strategy, and monetization across home help, cooks, and beauty verticals. His mandate focuses on scaling demand across Snabbit's nanomarkets through hyper-local planning and brand building. The hire follows the recent appointments of Chief Business Officer Abhinav Ankur and Operations Head Pradeep Yadav, bolstering Snabbit's leadership team as the company expands across five major urban centers after surpassing 10 million completed jobs. MathWorks and MapmyIndia Mappls partner to Accelerate ADAS validation for India MathWorks has partnered with MapmyIndia Mappls to integrate high-definition maps into MATLAB, Simulink, and RoadRunner workflows, enabling automotive engineers to simulate and validate Advanced Driver Assistance Systems for Indian driving conditions. By capturing local nuances like lane-level geometry, variable traffic, potholes, speed breakers, and faded markings, the integration creates realistic digital twins of complex road environments. This allows engineering teams to test ADAS controllers early using Model-Based Design, reducing reliance on expensive physical testing and accelerating the deployment of automotive safety technologies built specifically for India’s unique traffic ecosystems. Indian Specialty Coffee Debuts Across Greece and Cyprus On International Coffee Day, Indian Ambassador Shri Ravi Shankar launched The Origin Box in Athens, introducing Indian specialty coffee to Europe. The initiative is a partnership between Karnataka-based venture The Coorg Coffee Club and Greek retailer Coffee Island, placing the curated collection in over 400 stores across Greece and Cyprus. Featuring five specially processed coffees—spanning Arabica, Canephora, and Excelsa—from five distinct Coorg estates, each lot is documented from harvest to roast and carries its grower’s name. This collaboration establishes Indian shade-grown coffee as a traceable, premium origin, showcasing its distinct flavor profile to European consumers.

title: Flipkart picks up minority stake in B2B travel startup TravClan
content: Ecommerce marketplace Flipkart has picked up a minority stake in global B2B travel tech startup TravClan. The move is designed to upgrade international holiday packages and expand supply on both Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel. TravClan said it plans to use the new capital to scale its platform, deepen its global supply relationships, and expand its engineering, business development, and operational teams. Through the deal, Flipkart taps into TravClan's network of direct global suppliers and on-ground teams. TravClan currently powers outbound travel for over 15,000 travel agents, helping them build customised itineraries, book hotels, and handle activities with 24/7 destination support. Integrating these operations allows Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel to offer Indian travelers more curated international trips with reliable support throughout their journey. "Investing in TravClan strengthens our ability to offer international holiday packages while deepening our travel capabilities. Travellers today are looking for more than a flight or hotel booking. They want a holiday that is curated around their interests and supported throughout the journey. TravClan’s supplier network and destination capabilities will help us build that experience across Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel,” said Nishant Verman, SVP, Corporate Development and Partnerships, Flipkart. "India is becoming one of the largest outbound travel markets in the world, with travellers taking their first international trips driving a significant part of this growth. The opportunity lies in making these trips more affordable while maintaining reliable service levels. By contracting directly with suppliers and operating our own ground teams, we are able to offer competitive prices and deliver a consistent experience," said Arun Bagaria, Co-founder and CEO, TravClan. "This partnership with Flipkart allows us to take affordable travel products to millions of Indians as they embark on their international journeys," he added. Edited by Megha Reddy

title: PanIIT, Andhra Pradesh plan Rs 500 Cr deeptech fund, target 25 AP startups by 2030
content: PanIIT Alumni India and the Andhra Pradesh government plan to create a ₹500-crore venture fund focused on deeptech companies, as part of a broader effort to channel capital, research and manufacturing activity into the state. The proposed PanIIT Amaravati Venture Fund will seek capital from IIT alumni, industry and institutional investors and is targeting its first close by July 1, 2027, according to plans presented at the PanIIT Andhra Pradesh Summit in Vijayawada on Saturday. The fund aims to back at least 25 Andhra Pradesh-based deeptech ventures by 2030. The precise structure of the fund, including the respective financial commitments of PanIIT, the Andhra Pradesh government and private investors, was not immediately clear. Principal R&D or manufacturing in AP At least 50% of the companies the fund invests in will be expected to locate their principal R&D or manufacturing operations in Andhra Pradesh, according to material presented at the conference. The localisation requirement is designed to ensure that the proposed fund does more than invest in companies headquartered elsewhere, by tying a significant part of its portfolio to research or manufacturing activity within the state. Speaking to a panel of venture capital investors at the summit, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu made a direct pitch for investors to bring both capital and expertise. “You bring money, you bring mentors. I will match your contribution,” Naidu said. The precise mechanism through which the state would match private contributions, and whether the commitment would flow directly into the PanIIT Amaravati Venture Fund, was not immediately clear. The proposed fund seeks to address two constraints that frequently confront deeptech startups: access to patient capital and access to experienced operators and industry networks. Deeptech companies typically face longer product-development cycles and greater capital requirements than software-first startups, particularly in areas such as semiconductors, quantum technologies, aerospace, defence, healthcare and advanced manufacturing. Amaravati Declaration The venture fund sits within a broader framework laid out under the Andhra PanIIT Declaration, which seeks to create a long-term institutional relationship between the IIT ecosystem, industry and the Andhra Pradesh government. Among the proposed initiatives is a permanent PanIIT Amaravati Council, which is expected to act as a coordinating platform for deeptech, research and innovation initiatives in the state. The framework also includes a technology-transfer pipeline to identify research from IITs that can be commercialised in Andhra Pradesh, a 100-member global IIT mentor network and 10 industry chairs across universities and institutions in the state. The Amaravati Council is intended to connect IIT alumni, startups, universities, industry and policymakers and provide a more permanent structure for initiatives emerging from the summit. The broader framework also seeks to deepen collaboration between universities and industry, support startup creation and make it easier for research developed within the IIT ecosystem to move towards commercial deployment. It also sets a target of incubating at least 50 startups in Andhra Pradesh by 2030. IIT mentor network PanIIT is looking to build a mentor network alongside the fund. A proposed 100-member Global IIT Mentor Networkis expected to connect founders with IIT alumni who can provide guidance across product development, go-to-market strategy, scaling and execution. An initial cohort of 25 deeptech startups is expected to be matched with mentors, according to plans presented at the summit. The mentor network is intended to complement the proposed venture fund by bringing operating experience and industry connections alongside capital. Taken together, the fund, mentor network and Amaravati Declaration mark an attempt to link venture capital with IIT research and alumni expertise, while using Andhra Pradesh as a base for startup creation, R&D and manufacturing.

title: Why did Virat Kohli give up a Rs 300 Cr Puma deal to back Abhishek Ganguly’s Agilitas?
content: For 17 years, Abhishek Ganguly helped build one of the biggest sportswear success stories in India. When he joined Puma in 2005, he was the second employee in the country. The company did not even have an Indian entity, and its early team worked out of a Coffee World in Koramangala, Bengaluru, attracted partly by the free internet. Puma would eventually become one of the first single brands in fashion and sportswear to cross Rs 1,500 crore and then Rs 2,000 crore in revenue in India. Ganguly says it went on to become bigger than Nike and Adidas put together in the country. Perhaps even more striking was the capital behind that growth. According to Ganguly, by 2023, Puma India had put in only around $20 million in equity capital to build a business generating roughly $400 million in revenue. But when Ganguly decided to start Agilitas Sports, he realised that nearly two decades of experience could be as much a liability as an advantage. “What got Puma to where it got will not get Agilitas even an inch ahead,” he told Amit Somani, Managing Partner at Prime Venture Partners, on the Prime Venture Partners Podcast. Why India needs a different sportswear company The idea behind Agilitas came partly from something Ganguly had noticed during his years working for a global sportswear company. At Puma’s headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Germany, meeting rooms carried the names of cities including Barcelona, New York, Los Angeles, Tokyo, Melbourne and Seoul. “No New Delhi, no Bangalore,” he recalls. Rather than viewing it as a complaint, Ganguly saw an opportunity. Despite the growth of the Indian market, India did not yet have what he calls a “pride of place” in global sportswear. Countries such as the US and Germany had created global sports brands of their own. China had built its own brands too. Ganguly began asking a simple question: why not India? That question would eventually become central to Agilitas. “We always didn't want to be a brand for India. We wanted to be a brand from India,” he says. The distinction matters. Ganguly does not want Agilitas to compete by positioning Indian products as cheaper alternatives to international brands. His ambition is to build products that can compete with the best globally on their own terms. “This will compete with the best in the world,” he says of the company's products. ‘Consumers don’t need more brands’ Building that company, however, requires understanding how dramatically the Indian consumer has changed. Two decades ago, Ganguly says, consumers were reluctant to spend Rs 5,000 to Rs 6,000 on a pair of shoes. Today, sneaker culture has reached a point where he knows people in India who own as many as 400 pairs. Retail has transformed alongside the consumer. India moved from limited offline retail to mono-brand stores, ecommerce and now quick commerce. Consumers who once struggled to access international brands can today choose from an enormous range of products. That creates a very different problem for a company like Agilitas. “Consumers don't need more products, they don't need more brands, they don't need more retail,” Ganguly says. Availability alone is no longer differentiation. Neither is simply making another good shoe. Brands increasingly need to give consumers a reason to pay attention to them. Ganguly borrows a framework from social media to explain how he thinks about this. Instagram, he says, taught brands that content first needs to be “scroll stopping” and then good enough to be shared. “So there is a scroll stopping behavior and then you have to build which is shareable,” he says. “Scroll stopping means you got the attention, then you were good enough that people shared.” For Agilitas, the challenge is therefore not simply making products. It is earning consideration in a market where consumers already have plenty of choices. Why experience can become a founder’s biggest risk Perhaps Ganguly's most counterintuitive belief about building Agilitas is that his previous success does not necessarily give the company an advantage. It could do precisely the opposite. “The biggest risk Agilitas has is because I have done this before,” he says. His reasoning is that successful operators can become prisoners of their own pattern recognition. What worked previously starts looking like a template for what should work again. Confidence can turn into certainty, and certainty can reduce the willingness to learn. “If you think you know it, you build ego and you're low on learning,” he says. Ganguly has a phrase he says he reminds himself of every day: “Disruptors don't disrupt again.” The lesson has become particularly relevant because of the speed at which Indian consumption is changing. Ganguly says his first two-and-a-half to three years building Agilitas have already taught him things that run counter to lessons from his previous 20 years in the industry. Consumers are evolving too quickly, he argues, for history alone to provide the answers. From Virat Kohli the ambassador to Virat Kohli the builder One of the most visible manifestations of the Agilitas strategy is its relationship with Virat Kohli. The relationship goes back to 2016, when Kohli was Indian cricket captain and coming off an extraordinary IPL season. Ganguly, then at Puma, proposed something different from the conventional celebrity endorsement model. Rather than simply paying Kohli a fixed brand ambassador fee, he suggested building a brand that belonged to Kohli, which could collaborate with Puma through a royalty arrangement. That relationship eventually developed into One8. Years later, when Ganguly was preparing to leave Puma, Kohli was among the first people he told. Ganguly explained his ambition to create a sportswear company from India. The conversation returned to the same question behind Agilitas: “Why not us?” “Why can't an Indian brand get to the podium of the Olympics?” Ganguly recalls them asking. Why could a brand from India not eventually become the preferred choice of athletes elsewhere in the world? Kohli subsequently became one of Agilitas' early believers. Ganguly says the cricketer walked away from a large financial outlay from Puma, invested in Agilitas and merged his brand with the company. His role, Ganguly insists, goes considerably beyond lending his name and face to the brand. When the company was developing its first performance cricket shoe ahead of the IPL, Kohli personally tested the product and rejected 17 prototypes. “He tested it like, like with schoolboy energy,” Ganguly says, describing Kohli as being involved in the smallest details of the product. It is an example of what Agilitas wants the relationship to represent. Kohli is not merely the celebrity used to generate attention for a finished product. He is part of the process of building it. Building something that eventually outgrows its founders The long-term ambition is bigger than any individual associated with the company. Ganguly recalls asking Kohli what success for One8 would look like 20 years from now. Kohli's answer surprised him. Success, he said, would be when “nobody cares two hoots about who built this, who started this.” For Ganguly, that reflected a “deep builder mindset”. It also fits his own decision to start again. Ganguly grew up, he says, in an India where success was often associated with certainty and stability. People were encouraged to find a path and eventually “settle down”. Over time, he discovered that the moments he enjoyed most came from moving away from what had already been built and attempting something that had not been done before. “I want to stay unfinished till I can,” he says. For someone who has already spent two decades building in Indian sportswear, Agilitas is therefore less about recreating the last journey than attempting an entirely different one. And Ganguly's advice to entrepreneurs reflects that distinction. “Always learn from others. The gateway of the world is through others, but never try to copy others,” he says.
